--- lecture: "13a" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Statistical Methods]{.blue} Polynomial Regression ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | Course {{< meta course >}}]{}
[{{< meta instructor >}} | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ::: {.my-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![](../../img/growth_curve_357EDD.png){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Overview ## Motivation {.f6} - So far, we have always fit [straight lines]{.b} between $y$ and $x$ variables - But sometimes the correct functional form is [curved]{.b .red} in some way - If we fit a straight line anyway, our results may be very biased ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2023) df1 <- tibble( x = runif(100, -5, 5), y1 = 0.2 + 1.2*x + rnorm(100, 0, 1) ) df2 <- tibble( x = runif(100, -5, 5), y2 = 0.2 + 1.2*x - 0.5*x^2 + rnorm(100, 0, 2) ) p1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y1)) + geom_point(size = 2) + # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, # formula = y ~ x + I(x^2)) + # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5, # formula = y ~ x) + mytheme(20) p2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x, y2)) + geom_point(size = 2, color = "red") + # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, # formula = y ~ x + I(x^2)) + # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5, # formula = y ~ x) + mytheme(20) (p1 | p2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Linear regression ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- lm(y2 ~ x, data = df2) # data from right panel of slide 3 model_parameters(fit) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(98) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -4.54 | 0.43 | [-5.39, -3.70] | -10.66 | < .001 ## x | 1.19 | 0.14 | [ 0.90, 1.47] | 8.29 | < .001 r2(fit) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.412 ## adj. R2: 0.406 ``` ::: ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggeffects) plot(predict_response(fit, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggeffects) plot(predict_response(fit, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + mytheme() + theme( plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Conclusions {.f6} - Linear regression did not work well for predicting $y_2$ - The functional form diagnostic looked bad for the latter - The $R^2$ for the latter was worse than we could do ::: {.fragment} - We need to change our functional form! - We need to allow a curve in our function - This is what polynomial regression does ::: # Polynomial Regression ## Power polynomials {.f5} - LM can handle simple curves through **power polynomial** transformations! - We will add predictors that are *power transformations* of other predictors $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 \color{red}{x^1} + b_2 \color{red}{x^2} + \cdots + b_d \color{red}{x^d}$$ - Each term has a **degree** equal to its exponent + e.g., $x^1$ is the *first* degree term and $x^2$ is the *second* degree term + Note that $x^1=x$ and $x^0=1$, which can be thought of as the intercept + The term with the highest exponent is the **highest degree term** + All other terms are referred to as the **lower degree terms** ## Number of bends {.f6} - The highest degree term determines the curve's overall shape + The number of bends is equal to $(d-1)$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d1 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = x^1) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = "Linear (d=1)") + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) d2 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = x^2) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = "Quadratic (d=2)") + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) d3 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, .1), y = -5*x + x^3) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = "Cubic (d=3)") + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) (d1 | d2 | d3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Direction of curvature {.f6} - The sign $(\pm)$ of the curve's highest degree term's slope
determines its **direction of curvature** (i.e., up or down) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qp <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = x^2) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", +1*x^2))) + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) qn <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = -x^2) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", -1*x^2))) + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) cp <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = x^3) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", +1*x^3))) + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) cn <- tibble(x = seq(-10, 10, 1), y = -x^3) |> ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_line(linewidth = 2, color = "darkblue") + labs(title = expression(paste("y = ", -1*x^3))) + mytheme(20) + theme(axis.text = element_blank()) (qp | qn | cp | cn) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Quadratic Regression ## Expanding the equation {.f6} - A quadratic relationship requires two predictors to represent $x$ $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x^1 + b_2 x^2$$ - The **highest** degree coefficient determines the overall shape + $b_2$: Does the curve bend up $(+)$, down $(-)$, or not at all $(0)$? ::: {.pv2} - The **lower** degree coefficients fine-tune the position and shape + $b_1$: What is the slope of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$? + $b_0$: What is the intercept of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$? ::: ## Quadratic regression 1 - We use the `I()` function to do math inside the formula ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit1b <- lm(y1 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df1) model_parameters(fit1b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 0.27 | 0.15 | [-0.02, 0.57] | 1.82 | 0.072 ## x | 1.13 | 0.04 | [ 1.05, 1.20] | 30.43 | < .001 ## x^2 | 3.05e-03 | 0.01 | [-0.03, 0.03] | 0.21 | 0.838 r2(fit1b) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.908 ## adj. R2: 0.906 ``` ::: ::: {.f6} The $x^2$ slope is NOT significant, so the curve is NOT needed ::: ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit1b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit1b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit1b, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit1b, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + mytheme() + theme( plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Quadratic regression 2 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2b <- lm(y2 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df2) model_parameters(fit2b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -0.16 | 0.31 | [-0.77, 0.45] | -0.53 | 0.599 ## x | 1.27 | 0.07 | [ 1.13, 1.40] | 18.85 | < .001 ## x^2 | -0.50 | 0.03 | [-0.55, -0.44] | -18.71 | < .001 r2(fit2b) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.872 ## adj. R2: 0.870 ``` ::: - The $x^2$ slope is significant, so the curve is needed! - Because the slope is negative, it will bend downward ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit2b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit2b, terms = "x"), show_data = TRUE, dot_size = 3) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit2b, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit2b, check = "linearity", panel = FALSE))$NCV + mytheme() + theme( plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Visualizing the tangent line ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = y2)) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), linewidth = 1.5) + geom_abline( slope = 1.27, intercept = -0.16, color = "orange", linewidth = 2, alpha = 4/5 ) + annotate( geom = "label", x = 0, y = -12, label = "y = –0.16 + 1.27x", color = "orange", size = 7 ) + annotate( geom = "label", x = 0, y = -16, label = "y = –0.16 + 1.27x – 0.50x²", color = "blue", size = 7 ) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Calculating extrema - It may be useful to know the maximum or minimum values ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} What value of $x$ gives the
most extreme value of $y$? $$x_m = \frac{-b_1}{2b_2}$$ ::: ::: {.column} What is the most extreme value of $y$ in the function? $$\hat{y}_m = \frac{4 b_2 b_0 - b_1^2}{4 b_2}$$ ::: ::: ## Calculating extrema {.f90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_parameters(fit2b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -0.16 | 0.31 | [-0.77, 0.45] | -0.53 | 0.599 ## x | 1.27 | 0.07 | [ 1.13, 1.40] | 18.85 | < .001 ## x^2 | -0.50 | 0.03 | [-0.55, -0.44] | -18.71 | < .001 b_0 <- -0.16 b_1 <- 1.27 b_2 <- -0.50 x_m <- (-b_1) / (2 * b_2) x_m ## [1] 1.27 yhat_m <- ((4 * b_2 * b_0) - b_1^2) / (4 * b_2) yhat_m ## [1] 0.64645 ``` ::: ## Visualizing extrema ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = y2)) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), linewidth = 1.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.64645, color = "orange", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 4/5) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1.27, color = "orange", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 4/5) + annotate("label", x = 1.27, y = -17.5, label = "1.27", size = 7, color = "orange") + annotate("label", x = -3.75, y = 0.64645, label = "0.65", size = 7, color = "orange") + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Adding Predictors ## Adding another predictor {.f6} ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) salaries <- read_csv("../../data/salaries.csv") fit3 <- lm(salary ~ yrs.since.phd + I(yrs.since.phd^2) + sex, data = salaries) model_parameters(fit3) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(393) | p ## --------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 57.33 | 5.35 | [46.82, 67.85] | 10.72 | < .001 ## yrs since phd | 4.07 | 0.36 | [ 3.35, 4.78] | 11.20 | < .001 ## yrs since phd^2 | -0.06 | 7.22e-03 | [-0.08, -0.05] | -8.90 | < .001 ## sex [Male] | 9.11 | 4.28 | [ 0.70, 17.53] | 2.13 | 0.034 ``` ::: - The effects of `yrs.since.phd` are significant controlling for sex - The effect of `sex` is significant controlling for `yrs.since.phd` and its square ## Visualizing the model {.f90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit3, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex")), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit3, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex")), show_data = TRUE) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Adding moderation {.f6} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit4 <- lm( salary ~ yrs.since.phd + I(yrs.since.phd^2) + sex + yrs.since.phd:sex + I(yrs.since.phd^2):sex, data = salaries ) model_parameters(fit4) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(391) | p ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 65.02 | 12.60 | [ 40.24, 89.80] | 5.16 | < .001 ## yrs since phd | 2.95 | 1.50 | [ -0.00, 5.90] | 1.96 | 0.050 ## yrs since phd^2 | -0.03 | 0.04 | [ -0.11, 0.04] | -0.90 | 0.367 ## sex [Male] | 0.91 | 13.29 | [-25.21, 27.03] | 0.07 | 0.946 ## yrs since phd × sex [Male] | 1.18 | 1.55 | [ -1.86, 4.22] | 0.76 | 0.447 ## yrs since phd^2 × sex [Male] | -0.03 | 0.04 | [ -0.11, 0.05] | -0.79 | 0.432 ``` ::: - The effects of `yrs.since.phd` are not moderated by sex ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit4, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(predict_response(fit4, terms = c("yrs.since.phd", "sex"))) + mytheme() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Closing Thoughts ## Consider the range - You may only see *part* of the curve in your sample! ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Advice {.f6} - Models with higher degrees are more flexible + But they may overfit (fail to generalize) + They will be harder to interpret and justify - **Theory** should be used to decide between shapes + Quadratics can model processes with best/worst regions + Cubics can model opponent processes and regulation - Centering your $x$ variable is very helpful here + Also see `poly()` for orthogonal polynomials - Don't omit the lower degree terms/coefficients

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
